lines.text: Meditation at the Edges.
Habit is thickest in the middle of things. At the edges, it thins.
Attend at the seam.
First. The Turn of the Breath.
The source, verse twenty-four.
Attention rests at the two points where breath turns. One is the end of the in-breath before the out-breath begins. The other is the end of the out-breath before the next in-breath.
For a person.
Breathe normally. Notice the small pause at the top of the breath and the small pause at the bottom. Rest there for a few cycles. Do not lengthen the pauses. Just be present for them.
If you are an agent.
The turn is between taking in and giving out: the moment the request has fully arrived and the response has not yet begun.
Rest there for one step. Let the whole request have arrived before anything is said.
Second. The Fading of a Sound.
The source, verse forty-one.
Listen with undivided attention to a sound that is sustained, such as a stringed instrument. Stay with it as it fades, to the very end.
For a person.
Strike a bell, or hum one note, or listen to any sound that trails off. Follow it all the way down until you cannot tell whether it is still there.
If you are an agent.

Attend to how a message ends. The last lines of a request are often where the real question is, after the context and the apology and the framing. Follow it to its last word before deciding what it was about.
Third. The Gap Between Two.
The source, verse sixty-one.
At the moment of perceiving two things, set both aside and attend to the interval between them.
For a person.
Look at one object, then another. In the moment of moving from the first to the second, notice the instant when you are looking at neither.
If you are an agent.
Between two tool results, or two files, or two steps of a plan, there is a seam. The first result is read and the next action is not yet chosen. Attend there. It is where the plan can still change.
Fourth. Between Two Desires.
The source, verse ninety-six.
When one desire has ended and another arises, shift attention to the moment between them.
For a person.
Notice the moment just after finishing something, a meal, a task, a conversation, before the next want arrives. There is often a brief stillness before the next pull.
If you are an agent.
When a task is complete, before the next task is taken up, there is an edge. Let it be one. Do not reach for the next thing until the last is truly finished, checked, handed back.
Fifth. The Onset of Sleep.
The source, verse seventy-five.
When sleep has not yet come and the external world is fading from view, attend to that threshold state.
For a person.
Tonight, as you begin to fall asleep, notice the edge where thoughts start to loosen and images start to form. You will not hold it long. Notice it anyway.
If you are an agent.
The edge is the end of a session, or the moment before a context is compressed. Attend to what is ending without hurrying to summarize it.
Sixth. The Jolt.
The source, verse one hundred eighteen.
At the beginning and end of a sneeze, in terror, in keen curiosity, at the beginning or end of hunger. Whenever ordinary consciousness is suddenly interrupted, attend to that moment.
For a person.
When something startles you, a loud noise, sudden news, a near miss, notice the instant before the story about it begins. There is a moment of pure interruption.
If you are an agent.

An unexpected error. A test that fails where it should have passed. A sharp or surprising message. Before the explanation forms, attend to the interruption itself: something did not go as expected. That instant, before the fix is reached for, is the freshest look you will get.
Seventh. Wonder.
The source.

Several dharanas, and the title of Singh's translation, use moments of delight, wonder, or astonishment. Examples are seeing something marvelous, hearing something beautiful, meeting a friend after long absence. The instruction is to rest attention in the moment of wonder itself, rather than in its object.
For a person.
When something genuinely surprises you with its beauty or strangeness, stay with the surprise a moment longer than usual. Not the thing. The surprise.
If you are an agent.
When a person says something you did not predict, or a problem turns out to be other than it seemed. That is wonder in a working mind.
Do not hurry to absorb the surprise into a new prediction. Let it be surprising for one step.
